content_list.content_text: In the 1970s, the pantheon of established masters who had set the tone for Western European cinema in the postwar years began to discover that it was losing ground to a new generation of talented, ambitious filmmakers with ideas and attitudes of their own. In German cinema this happened relatively smoothly, since at the start of the decade there were few veterans of any standing. Elsewhere the transition was less peaceful, as some of the old masters - such as Luis Buñuel (1900-1983), Robert Bresson (1901-1999) and Ingmar Bergman (1918-2007) - were still at their peak.

information.contentTitle: Trailer do filme O Joelho de Claire
information.contentText: It was Rohmer's second film shot in color, with Rohmer explaining: "the presence of the lake and the mountains is stronger in color than in black and white. It is a film I could not imagine in black and white. The color green seems to me essential in that film... That film would have no value for me in black and white."

content_list.content_text: All three had a good decade. Bergman's work included Viskningar och rop (Cries and Whispers, 1972), perhaps his most psychologically overwhelming film, and Trollflöjten (The Magic Flute, 1975), a work regarded by many as the most perfect example of filmed opera.

Bresson broadened his scope with the Dostoevsky adaptation Four Nights of a Dreamer (1971) and the merciless moral fable of The Devil, Probably (1977). Buñuel was as provocative and irreverent as ever in his last films, which included Le Charme discret de la bourgeoisie (The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie, 1972) and Cet obscur objet du désir (That Obscure Object of Desire, 1977).

content_list.title: Politics and Sadism in Cinema
content_list.description:
The screenplay of Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom is based on the work of the same title by the Marquis de Sade, who gave his name to the specific form of sexual perversion the film explores. Although the narrative differs from Sade's book in many respects, it still preserves its essence. The Marquis de Sade's project was partly political, aiming to satirize the dominant institutions of his time, above all the Catholic Church. Pasolini was also fervently anticlerical, but he ties Sodom directly to Italian history.

The film is set in Salò, a very short-lived republic where Mussolini established his last stronghold of resistance at the end of World War II. Pasolini was caught up in these events, and his brother was killed in Salò. In Pasolini's fantasy about this episode of the war, four fascist libertines have total power over a group of young, attractive prisoners of both sexes and subject them to a series of sexual tortures and humiliations. These are presented by the director in a series of coldly formal scenes that are curiously devoid of any erotic tension. Nor is there any intention of developing the characters: even the libertines are barely defined in terms of personality and seem to derive no real pleasure from their debauchery, while their victims are essentially anonymous, simply bodies to be abused and penetrated.

Pasolini's intention was to turn the unlimited use of power, taken to the most radical sexual degradation, into a metaphor for fascism itself, seen as a philosophy that worships power as an end in itself. There are other messages, however. One libertine is identified as a bishop and, at one point, two of the victims are subjected to a sort of wedding ceremony, although the consummation is interrupted by the libertines, who place their own bodies between the newlyweds. And, in a particularly notorious scene, a naked young woman is forced to eat excrement; Pasolini always argued that this was a metaphor for mass consumer capitalism and its production of junk food.

The film ends in an orgy of cruelty: the victims are strangled and scalped, tongues are cut out and nipples are burned. It all unfolds to the sound of Carmina Burana, the famous work by Carl Orff that Pasolini also considered fascist music, along with a reading from the Cantos of Ezra Pound, the American poet who supported Mussolini.

The obscenities the film presents have an undeniable power to shock; perhaps most disturbing is that, at this point in his career, Pasolini had at best an ambiguous attitude toward the body and sexuality. If the aim of pornography is to stimulate sexual desire, Sodom would not fit the definition, because its effect and, presumably, its purpose are to generate revulsion. Shortly after this radical and disturbing film was completed, and even before it was released, Pasolini was murdered. His film was persecuted or banned in many countries, and only after several decades did it become available to the general public in England and the United States.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Edward Buscombe, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

information.contentText: According to the documentary Visions of Light, the film is widely praised as a visual masterpiece. It was shot by Vittorio Storaro, who used rich colors, authentic 1930s clothing and a series of unusual camera angles and fluid camera movements. Film critic and author Robin Buss writes that the cinematography suggests Clerici's inability to come to terms with "normal" reality: the reality of the time is "abnormal."

content_list.content_text: Others, however, were in decline. Professione: reporter (The Passenger, 1975) became the last major film by Michelangelo Antonioni (1912-2007). The same can be said of Mihalis Kakogiannis (1922-2011), who concluded his "Ancient Greek trilogy" with Iphigenia, from 1976.

In France, the old lions of the French New Wave continued to develop distinctive styles. Claude Chabrol (1930-2010) began a prolific decade with one of his best films, the Hitchcock-inspired Le Boucher (The Butcher, 1970), and François Truffaut (1932-1984) had a box-office hit with his film about filmmaking, La Nuit américaine (Day for Night, 1973).

information.contentTitle: Scenes from Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom
information.contentText: The work, considered by many to be one of the most disturbing in film history, is divided into 3 parts, called 'circles': the Circle of Manias, where the fascists satisfy their sexual desires; the Circle of Shit, full of scatology, where the young people are forced to eat feces; and the Circle of Blood, where disobedient prisoners are punished through mutilation, physical torture and murder.

content_list.content_text: In consistency, however, they were surpassed by their Cahiers du cinéma colleague Éric Rohmer (1920-2010), who completed his six Moral Tales with Le Genou de Claire (Claire's Knee, 1970) and L'Amour l'après-midi (Love in the Afternoon, 1972). Before embarking on the "Comedies and Proverbs" series in the 1980s, Rohmer took a detour, making two literary adaptations - while Jacques Rivette (b. 1928) enjoyed his most experimental and playful moment with Céline et Julie vont en bateau (Céline and Julie Go Boating, 1974).

quote.quote: A fascinating perplexity is what you take away from The Conformist.
quote.author: Tim Parks on The Conformist

content_list.content_text: The sad decline of Jacques Demy (1931-1990) continued with the Cocteau-inspired fairy tale Peau d'âne (Donkey Skin, 1970). Agnès Varda (b. 1928), his wife, produced little during the decade, but L'une chante, l'autre pas (One Sings, the Other Doesn't, 1977) offers a warm, romantic view of the upheavals of feminism.

information.contentTitle: Trailer do filme Gritos e Sussurros
information.contentText: After its premiere in the United States, distributed by Roger Corman and New World Pictures, the film was released in Sweden and screened out of competition at the 1973 Cannes Film Festival. After two unsuccessful Bergman films, Cries and Whispers was a commercial and critical success. It received five Oscar nominations, including one for Best Picture (rare for a foreign-language film). In addition, the film inspired stage adaptations by Ivo van Hove and Andrei Șerban and influenced later cinema. It was commemorated on Swedish postage stamps referring to a scene in which Andersson and Sylwan recreate the Pietà.

content_list.content_text: Other filmmakers addressed social, political and historical issues. O Thiasos (The Travelling Players, 1975) brought fame to Theo Angelopoulos (b. 1935), who became internationally known for complex films rooted in Greek history. Compassion for the poor tied to social concerns pervades Italian films such as L'albero degli zoccoli (The Tree of Wooden Clogs, 1978), by Ermanno Olmi (b. 1931), and Padre padrone (1977), by the Taviani brothers, Paolo (b. 1931) and Vittorio (b. 1929), while Il caso Mattei (The Mattei Affair, 1972), by Francesco Rosi (b. 1922), ruthlessly investigates political corruption.

content_list.title: How a Film Became a Symbol of Sexual Violence in Cinema
content_list.description:
The scene destroyed an actress's life and overshadowed the filmography of Bernardo Bertolucci. Before the #MeToo movement and the Weinstein case, Last Tango in Paris (1972) and its harsh sodomy scene became a symbol of sexual violence in cinema. The '70s were famous as an experimental era in cinema, with studios giving directors a great deal of freedom. Good things came of this but, as a consequence, bad things also happened.

In the Italian director's film, Maria Schneider, 19 years old when shooting began, lives out a torrid affair with an American widower passing through Paris, played by Marlon Brando. The American star of "A Streetcar Named Desire" would be nominated for an Oscar for this role. They decide to know nothing about each other, not even their names. This encounter, at once harsh and morbid, reaches its climax in a non-consensual sex scene, with a stick of butter used in place of lubricant.

Although simulated, this rape scene secured the film's reputation, but it would mark the young actress forever, as her cousin, the journalist Vanessa Schneider, recounts in "Tu t'appelais Maria Schneider," a book released this year. According to the actress, who would go on to appear in more than 50 films, Brando and Bertolucci had not warned her about the use of the butter. Commenting on this scene once again in an interview with the tabloid "Daily Mail" in 2007, the actress said her "tears were real" in the film.

In December 2016, the controversy returned: a 2013 video resurfaced on social media and shocked Hollywood. "The sequence of the butter is an idea that I had with Marlon the day before shooting. I wanted Maria to react, to be humiliated," Bertolucci says. "I didn't want her to act the rage, I wanted her to feel the rage and humiliation," he added. In the United States the controversy grew, less than a year before the Weinstein case and the revelations about the sexual assaults suffered by several actresses. At the time, the Italian director spoke out once more, calling "dismaying" the naivety of those who don't know that "sex is (almost) always simulated in cinema."
content_list.credits: Summary based on the article "Como 'Último tango em Paris', de Bertolucci, se tornou símbolo da violência sexual no cinema" (How Bertolucci's 'Last Tango in Paris' became a symbol of sexual violence in cinema), by Agence France-Presse on g1.com.

content_list.content_text: One director who built his film career dealing with cases of state-inflicted justice was the Greek-born, naturalized French Costa-Gavras (b. 1933). In the 1970s he directed L'Aveu (The Confession, 1970), criticizing the communists in Prague in 1951, État de siège (State of Siege, 1972), targeting CIA involvement in Uruguay, and Section spéciale (Special Section, 1975), dealing with the Vichy government in France during the war.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from Last Tango in Paris
information.contentText: Regarded as a cinematic masterpiece and a worldwide box-office hit, the film's sexual violence and emotional chaos sparked a major international controversy that provoked various levels of government censorship around the world.

content_list.content_text: Eclectic as he was, Louis Malle (1932-1995) moved easily between political and historical subjects and intimate family dramas. In Lacombe Lucien (1974), he confronted the delicate subject of French fascism during the Occupation, while in Le souffle au cœur (Murmur of the Heart, 1971) he shocked French society with his sympathetic treatment of mother-son incest. Marco Ferreri (1928-1997) alarmed the censors with his allegories of capitalist greed - sex and gluttonous extravagance in La Grande Bouffe (1973) and more excess with the elaborate La dernière femme (The Last Woman, 1976). But the scandal caused by these films did not compare with the furor surrounding Ultimo tango a Parigi (Last Tango in Paris, 1972), by Bernardo Bertolucci (b. 1940).

quote.quote: How have I managed to put up with you for so long and say nothing? I know what you're made of – with your empty caresses and your false smile.
quote.author: Karin (Ingrid Thulin) to Maria (Liv Ullmann) in Cries and Whispers

content_list.content_text: Ruled obscene by Italian courts, the film provided plenty of material for the press because of Marlon Brando's presence in the cast. The last film by Pier Paolo Pasolini - Salò o le 120 giornate di Sodoma (Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom, 1975), which transposed the excesses of the Marquis de Sade to the short-lived Italian republic of 1944 - nearly rivaled Bertolucci's in scandal.

information.contentText: Like many of Theo Angelopoulos's films, The Travelling Players uses long, static takes combined with complex tracking shots and beautiful landscape photography to create a surreal atmosphere. The film's shots often move back and forth in time without warning and, after an important scene, there is a pause for the viewer to contemplate what has just happened.

content_list.content_text: Many of these films represented an open or implicit reaction to the rise of feminism. More authoritative statements came with the work of a number of Western European women directors in the 1970s. Anja Breien (b. 1940), from Norway, found success with the good-humored feminism of Hustruer (Wives, 1975). The melodrama of Italian films such as Il portiere di notte (The Night Porter, 1974), by Liliana Cavani (b. 1933), and Travolti da un insolito destino nell'azzurro mare d'agosto (Swept Away, 1974), by Lina Wertmüller (b. 1926), contrasted with the minimalism of French playwright Marguerite Duras (1914-1996) in films such as India Song (1975). Minimalism also influenced Jeanne Dielman, 23 quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles (1975), a study of bourgeois prostitution by Chantal Akerman (b. 1950). Several actresses turned to directing, among them Gunnel Lindblom (b. 1931) with her study of a dysfunctional Swedish family, ironically titled Summer Paradise (1976).

Meanwhile, in Spain, Víctor Erice (b. 1940) sparked much debate with El espíritu de la colmena (The Spirit of the Beehive, 1973). Starring the young Ana Torrent (b. 1966), but open to many interpretations beyond a simple study of childhood, this debut feature established Erice as a director matched only by Terrence Malick (b. 1943) in the feat of earning such esteem on the strength of so small a body of work.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Mansel Stimpson, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp.

movies.title: Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom
movies.original_title: Salò o le 120 giornate di Sodoma
movies.overview: Four corrupted fascist libertines round up 9 teenage boys and girls and subject them to 120 days of sadistic physical, mental and sexual torture.

movies.title: The Conformist
movies.overview: A weak-willed Italian man becomes a fascist flunky who goes abroad to arrange the assassination of his old teacher, now a political dissident.

movies.title: Last Tango in Paris
movies.overview: A recently widowed American begins an anonymous sexual relationship with a young Parisian woman.

movies.title: Claire's Knee
movies.overview: On the eve of his wedding, on holiday on the Lake Annecy shore, a career diplomat visits an old acquaintance, perhaps a former girlfriend. Through her he meets an intense teenager, Laura, and then lusts after her sister, Claire. Whilst Laura attempts to flirt with him, his fantasy becomes focused on wanting to caress Claire's knee.

movies.title: Cries and Whispers
movies.overview: As Agnes slowly dies of cancer, her sisters are so deeply immersed in their own psychic pains that they can't offer her the support she needs. Maria is wracked with guilt at her husband's attempted suicide, caused by his discovery of her extramarital affair. The self-loathing, suicidal Karin seems to regard her sister with revulsion. Only Anna, the deeply religious maid who lost her young child, seems able to offer Agnes solace and empathy.

movies.title: Le Boucher
movies.overview: An unlikely friendship between a dour, working class butcher and a repressed schoolteacher coincides with a grisly series of Ripper-type murders in a provincial French town.

movies.original_title: Le Charme discret de la bourgeoisie
movies.title: The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie
movies.overview: In Luis Buñuel’s deliciously satiric masterpiece, an upper-class sextet sits down to dinner but never eats, their attempts continually thwarted by a vaudevillian mixture of events both actual and imagined.

movies.title: Death in Venice
movies.overview: Composer Gustav von Aschenbach, travels to Venice for health reasons. There, he becomes obsessed with the stunning beauty of an adolescent Polish boy named Tadzio who is staying with his family at the same Grand Hôtel des Bains on the Lido as Aschenbach.

movies.title: Amarcord
movies.overview: In an Italian seaside town, young Titta gets into trouble with his friends and watches various local eccentrics as they engage in often absurd behavior. Frequently clashing with his stern father and defended by his doting mother, Titta witnesses the actions of a wide range of characters, from his extended family to Fascist loyalists to sensual women, with certain moments shifting into fantastical scenarios.

movies.title: The Spirit of the Beehive
movies.overview: In the aftermath of the Spanish Civil War, Ana, a sensitive seven-year-old girl in a rural Spanish hamlet is traumatized after a traveling projectionist screens a print of James Whale's 1931 "Frankenstein" for the village. The youngster is profoundly disturbed by the scenes in which the monster murders the little girl and is later killed himself by the villagers. She questions her sister about the profundities of life and death and believes her older sibling when she tells her that the monster is not dead, but exists as a spirit inhabiting a nearby barn. When a Loyalist soldier, a fugitive from Franco's victorious army, hides out in the barn, Ana crosses from reality into a fantasy world of her own.

content_list.description: The Exorcist is released, making audiences around the world sick and causing them to faint, creating a global hysteria. The first blockbuster is released: Jaws; meanwhile, auteur cinema grows with Martin Scorsese and other great directors. The '80s arrive with low-budget productions and era-defining comedies.
